newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar seen losing more ground to ringgit.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar seen losing more ground to ringgit.

text.p: The Singapore dollar is likely to be hurt further this year by a stronger Malaysian ringgit as Malaysia's higher yields and improved economic outlook lure away funds, economists and foreign exchange dealers said on Thursday.
"The ringgit definitely has much more potential for strength against the Singapore dollar," said Chia Woon Khien, an economist at the Union Bank of Switzerland.
"In the course of the next one year, we think 60 cents is a good level between the ringgit and Sing dollar based on the competitiveness between the two countries," she added.

Chia said the Singapore dollar showed scope to weaken to at least 1.4300 against the U.S. dollar in the first half of the year, as a slowdown in the city-state's export growth translated into weakness in its exchange rate.
The Singapore currency has fallen almost 2.5 percent against the ringgit since the start of this year, after strengthening against its neigbour around the end of last year,

The ringgit/Singapore dollar cross rate hit a five-month high of 0.5682 on Wednesday. It was quoted at 0.5671/78 in Asian morning trade on Thursday. The Singapore dollar stood at 1.4055/65 to the U.S. dollar in morning trade.
The ringgit was at 2.4755/65 against the dollar after hitting a 17-month high of 2.4680 on January 13.
Andy Tan, economist at MMS International, said the ringgit/Singapore dollar cross showed scope to reach an initial target of 0.5700 and then head for the next target at 0.5750.
"It's too early to say the ringgit/Sing's current bull phase is over because we haven't seen any sign of strong profit-taking in the cross yet," Tan said.

He said an interest rate differential of more than 400 basis points between the benchmark three-month interbank rates of Singapore and Malaysia, in the latter's favour, was an obvious reason behind the recent rise in the cross rate.
But he added that Malaysia's positive economic growth outlook and prospects for a stronger ringgit were also factors.

"This year, there are more expectations the ringgit would strengthen and that could be another reason funds are going into the ringgit, to enjoy the interest yield as well as currency gain," Tan said.
But the Singapore dollar was unlikely to weaken beyond 1.4200 against its U.S. counterpart, despite the flows into the ringgit, he said.

"Fundamentally, there seem to be a lot more arguments for the ringgit, from interest rates not being lowered in the near term to economic stability," said Song Seng Wun, regional economist at H.G. Asia.
He said that although a large portion of the funds going into the ringgit were of a speculative nature, there was also increased investment in the Kuala Lumpur stock market.
Song said the ringgit/Singaore dollar cross could strengthen to 0.5800 but the Singapore dollar was likely to claw back some ground on any moves above that level.
However, a strategist with a large U.S. bank took a less bullish view of the ringgit's potential for further gains against both the Singapore and U.S. dollars.

"The ringgit/Sing cross has moved a lot since the start of the year. But from here, there's not too much more to go," he said, adding that the ringgit was also unlikely to strengthen beyond 2.4650 against the U.S. dollar.
